headline: Western governments weigh how to respond to China's export surge
body:
What happened: China's exports are growing fast, especially in new-economy goods such as electric vehicles and high-tech products, while its domestic factory activity has weakened. Coverage points to a growing dilemma for Western governments: welcome cheaper imports that help consumers, or shield local manufacturers from a flood of Chinese goods. Beijing also says it wants to expand its services exports, which could widen its trade footprint further. No specific market figures were confirmed in the material reviewed.

Reported by: Bloomberg. Also covered by Reuters, Nikkei Asia, China Daily.

headline: Poilievre to visit Washington seeking tariff-free trade with the US
body:
What happened: Pierre Poilievre, leader of Canada's Conservative Party, is set to travel to Washington next week to press for tariff-free trade with the United States. The headlines note the trip comes as Washington proposes fresh tariffs that have drawn pushback from several Asian trade partners, who are reportedly speeding up their own trade deals with the US. Asian stock markets were reported to be rising despite the tariff plan, while US stock futures edged higher in a holiday-thinned session with technology shares in focus. Canada, a major US trading partner, has a clear stake in any tariff outcome, though the headlines did not give details of specific rates or sectors affected.

Reported by: The Wall Street Journal. Also covered by Bloomberg, Financial Times, MarketWatch, BNN Bloomberg.

headline: IMF study weighs how China could shift to a new growth model
body:
What happened: The International Monetary Fund has published a study examining how China might move away from its current growth model toward a new one. The report assesses the structural forces behind the economy's expansion and the policy changes that could sustain growth as it matures. It is an IMF analytical publication rather than a news event, and its findings reflect the authors' assessment of China's economic data and policy trends over the period it covers.

The study's conclusions bear on China's own households, businesses and government, as well as on trading partners that depend on Chinese demand and investment. Because the report is an analysis, its recommendations are not policy decisions, and readers should consult the full document for the specific data, countries and time period it uses.

Reported by: IMF.

impactPoints: China's households and businesses would feel any shift in growth drivers toward consumption and productivity.
Trading partners that rely on Chinese demand and investment could be affected by a slower or rebalanced growth path.

headline: Study estimates gains from a 28th EU-wide company regime
body:
What happened: A study published by CEPR, the Centre for Economic Policy Research, examines how a 28th regime, an optional EU-wide legal framework for businesses alongside the national systems of the 27 member states, could help European firms grow to continental scale. The authors quantify the economic gains such a regime might bring. The analysis is framed as a quantitative estimate of potential benefits rather than a description of an enacted policy, and the summary here reflects the study's stated focus on the scale of possible gains for European firms.

The findings concern the European single market, where fragmentation across national rules is often cited as holding back firm growth. Businesses that want to operate across borders face separate rules, which the study links to smaller firms and lower productivity. Readers should check the full paper for the specific datasets, countries and time period used.

Reported by: CEPR (VoxEU).

impactPoints: European firms operating across borders could gain from a single optional company framework that reduces national rule differences.
The wider EU single market and member state economies would see the estimated productivity and growth effects of easier continental scaling.

headline: India says trade pact with US is close to finished
body:
What happened: India's commerce minister has said that a bilateral trade agreement with the United States is nearing completion. Talks are reportedly far along, and the outcome is being watched by exporters and investors on both sides. The reporting also points to a recent US tariff plan, which adds urgency for India to finalise terms. Officials have not been quoted as giving a firm signing date, so the timing remains uncertain. Markets and Indian exporters would stand to benefit from easier access to the large American consumer market.

Reported by: BNN Bloomberg. Also covered by Reuters, Bloomberg.

headline: Ratings agency S&P turns cautious on France's credit outlook
body:
What happened: S&P Global Ratings has lowered its outlook on France to negative, pointing to weak public finances and political uncertainty ahead of elections. The move signals that the agency sees a rising chance of a future downgrade of the country's credit rating unless fiscal discipline improves. Only the outlook has changed, not the rating itself.

For French borrowers and the government, the decision raises the prospect of higher costs when raising debt, and it puts pressure on Paris to show credible budget plans. Investors in French government bonds are likely to watch the move closely, as it can influence yields and wider European debt markets.

Reported by: Reuters. Also covered by Bloomberg, Financial Times.

headline: US corporate profits reach record share of GDP, raising sustainability doubts
body:
What happened: US corporate earnings have climbed to 13.37% of GDP in the third quarter, according to government figures released November 25, up from 13.14% in the prior quarter. Profits rose about 23% over the year to Q3 while nominal GDP grew roughly 6%, and strategists expect earnings to keep outpacing output into 2027. Analysts quoted by Fortune warn such peaks historically revert, citing workers seeking bigger shares of income and competition from cheaper AI chips. Separately, Volkswagen is fighting a $1.2 billion Indian tax demand, arguing rivals such as Mercedes-Benz and BMW use similar import practices.

Reported by: Bloomberg. Also covered by Reuters, CNA, Fortune, Yahoo Finance.

headline: Brazil's markets rally after Lula names banker as finance minister
body:
What happened: Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has appointed a banker from Bradesco as the country's finance minister, a move aimed at easing investor concerns about fiscal policy. Brazilian assets rallied after the announcement, with investors reading the choice as a sign of continuity and steadier economic management. The reporting covered in the headlines points to a market reaction in Brazil, though it does not give full details of the new minister's policy plans.

The appointment matters most to Brazilian markets and the businesses and households tied to them. International investors holding Brazilian stocks and bonds also gain from a calmer outlook, while the government hopes the choice will restore confidence.

Reported by: AP. Also covered by Bloomberg, Financial Times.

headline: Restricted Nvidia Blackwell chips found at Shanghai data centre linked to Huang
body:
What happened: Nvidia's Blackwell processors, which the US bars from China without a licence, have been found in a Shanghai data centre tied to Alice Huang, a woman linked to a controversy around the chipmaker. Documents filed with Chinese regulators and bank loan records show two Chinese firms listed a GB300 NVL72 rack and a GB200 server at the site. It is unclear how the hardware reached China, and Nvidia and Megaspeed did not respond to the findings. The case adds to pressure on Nvidia over diversion of its chips to China, a trade US officials believe is worth billions.

Reported by: Bloomberg. Also covered by The Telegraph, The Business Times, BNN Bloomberg.

headline: US tariffs on 14 trading partners spark debate over trade and retaliation
body:
What happened: The United States has announced tariffs of up to 20 percent on 14 major trading partners, including China and the European Union. The measures replace earlier levies that were struck down by the US Supreme Court, and commentators are debating why Washington is reintroducing them and how Beijing and others may respond. Indonesia, also among the 14, is negotiating in parallel with Washington, where a 19 percent tariff was set in a deal last year.

The tariffs add to pressure on trade flows and markets. Indonesia's stock index has fallen roughly 38 percent this year, and an index provider has proposed downgrading the country's market status, which Jakarta disputes. Meanwhile the EU and Indonesia signed a trade agreement, which Indonesia's economy minister said was accelerated partly by US tariff pressure.

Reported by: Euronews. Also covered by Al Jazeera, ABC News (Australia).

headline: Tech sectors lift China's industrial profits to a five-month high
body:
What happened: China's industrial profits rose at their fastest pace in five months, with the gain driven largely by technology-linked industries. Reporting indicates the recovery is still uneven, with some sectors lagging behind the stronger performers. The improvement points to new growth drivers filling gaps left by weaker traditional manufacturing.

For investors and trading partners, the data suggests firmer momentum in China's industrial economy, though analysts note the upturn is not yet broad-based. The figures are a signal watched by markets across Asia and beyond as China's economy weighs on global demand and commodity prices.

Reported by: Reuters. Also covered by Bloomberg, CNBC, Arab News, Xinhua.

headline: US goods trade gap widens as AI-related imports push purchases abroad higher
body:
What happened: The United States' goods trade deficit grew again, reaching a level that marks the fourth consecutive monthly widening. Imports climbed to a record, with the surge in artificial intelligence-related products cited as a major driver. Exports did not keep pace, so the gap between what the US buys from abroad and what it sells overseas expanded.

The data points to strong demand for computing hardware and related equipment, which is flowing mainly from Asian suppliers into American data centres and firms. Currency and bond markets typically watch such figures for signs of how much the US must borrow from abroad to fund its spending, though the report itself is a trade measure rather than a market-moving policy decision.

Reported by: Reuters. Also covered by Bloomberg, The Globe and Mail.

headline: UNCTAD's 2026 report examines foreign investment trends across Southeast Asia
body:
What happened: The UN Trade and Development agency, UNCTAD, has published its ASEAN Investment Report 2026, a study of investment flows across the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. The report is an analytical publication rather than a news event, and it covers the ten ASEAN member economies as a bloc as well as individually. It is intended to inform governments, investors and policymakers about where capital is moving in the region and what shapes those flows.

The findings concern the ASEAN member states and the foreign and domestic investors that operate within them. The report draws on UNCTAD's investment data and the region's economic records over the period it covers, and it is aimed at guiding investment policy and promotion across the bloc.

headline: Binance reopens withdrawals after recovery work on $6.3bn cyberattack
body:
What happened: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has finished recovering its withdrawal systems after a cyberattack last month that cost it about $6.3 billion in tokens. Withdrawals had been suspended for two days, and customers pulled a net $4.7 billion once they reopened on November 2. The exchange said nearly all networks are now open, with only a few paused for routine maintenance. About $2.85 billion of the stolen funds has been frozen by token issuers, while researchers say the rest is being moved through obscure services and could take months or years to trace.

Reported by: The National. Also covered by Reuters, CNA, The Globe and Mail.

headline: EU leaders face talks on long-term budget and Ukraine funding
body:

Member states remain divided over how much each should contribute and how the bloc's spending should be shared out. Officials are working towards a deal by December, but no agreement had been confirmed in the reporting. Ukraine's finances and the bloc's wider economic planning depend on the outcome, with markets watching for signs of how the union will fund its commitments.

Reported by: AP. Also covered by Bloomberg, BBC News, Al Jazeera, BNN Bloomberg.

headline: Nvidia shares surge as Jensen Huang returns as CEO
body:
What happened: Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive, and the company's stock jumped more than 30% to close at $165.05. The rally lifted the broader US market, with the S&P 500 up 4.7% and the Nasdaq up 6.5%, their best days since April 2025. The move recovered much of the drop that followed Huang's resignation on November 12, which came after he admitted to an affair and amid reports about a executive accused by US intelligence officials of passing information to China; Chinese officials called those claims fabricated. Huang's family foundation, which holds about 59 million Nvidia shares, gained roughly $2.3 billion in value in a single day.

Reported by: Reuters. Also covered by Bloomberg, BNN Bloomberg, SCMP, Yahoo Finance.

headline: Musk pledges SpaceX shares for US children, valued near $18 billion
body:
What happened: Elon Musk has pledged to give SpaceX shares to children across the United States, with the total value estimated at about $18 billion based on Wednesday's closing price of $127.44. SpaceX will contribute one new Class A share to each active Trump Account, with Musk matching that with his own shares. The company's transfer is due in December, while Musk's personal shares will not move until June 2027. The pledge comes as the Federal Communications Commission approved SpaceX plans for up to one million satellites to run solar-powered data centres in orbit, a decision astronomers criticised. Markets and analysts see it as a way to build a large retail shareholder base.

Reported by: Forbes. Also covered by Al Jazeera, The Telegraph.

Reports describe the move as unusual because the statement came at midday, and some outlets say Chinese equities posted their strongest gains in about two years. The rally lifted investor sentiment across the mainland market.

The move matters for foreign investors, global fund managers and China's exporters, since a firmer yuan and stronger share prices can ease financial conditions. Reports do not give detailed measures, so the scale of any future intervention remains unclear.

headline: UK's FTSE 100 set for strongest week in eight months
body:
What happened: Britain's FTSE 100 rose sharply on Thursday as Wall Street recovered most of its overnight losses. Earlier, a sell-off in shares of major artificial intelligence companies had hit the Nasdaq hard. Miners and banks led the London gains, and the index was on track for its best week in eight months. The rebound also reflected a wider recovery in global technology and mining stocks, with markets across the world steadying as volatility eased.

Reported by: Reuters. Also covered by Bloomberg, Nikkei Asia, MarketWatch, BNN Bloomberg.

headline: IMF board completes 2026 economic review of Australia
body:
What happened: The International Monetary Fund's Executive Board has wrapped up its 2026 Article IV consultation with Australia, an annual check on a member country's economic health. The review is the Fund's own assessment, drawing on discussions with Australian authorities and the Fund's standard surveillance analysis. No text beyond the headline was available, so the specific findings, data and time period covered cannot be confirmed here. headline: Tokyo core inflation hits 16-month high, boosting December rate-hike bets
body:
What happened: Core consumer prices in Tokyo rose 2.9 per cent in November from a year earlier, the fastest pace in 16 months and slightly below forecasts of 3.0 per cent. The reading, often seen as a preview of national trends, strengthens the case for the Bank of Japan to lift interest rates at its December 18 meeting. Price gains spread across food, daily goods and hotel charges, though the end of government utility subsidies also played a part. Most analysts polled by Reuters expected a December hike, though one economist warned market turmoil over AI and chips could lead the BOJ to hold off.

Reported by: Reuters. Also covered by Bloomberg, Nikkei Asia, CNA, Japan Times.

headline: Australia passes gas reservation law, LNG exporters warn of lasting uncertainty
body:
What happened: Australia's parliament has cleared a law requiring liquefied natural gas exporters to set aside about 20% of their supply for the domestic market, aimed at easing local shortages and bringing down prices. The measure follows an earlier delay in the final vote. Industry groups argue the rules will keep investors uncertain for a long time, which could weigh on future export projects and on global LNG buyers in Asia who rely on Australian supply. Exact implementation details were not confirmed in the reporting.

Reported by: Reuters. Also covered by Bloomberg, The Wall Street Journal, Nikkei Asia, Japan Times.

headline: Spain's Hernández de Cos poised to lead the European Central Bank
body:
What happened: Pablo Hernández de Cos, the governor of Spain's central bank, is reported to be on course to replace Christine Lagarde as president of the European Central Bank. The headlines from several outlets point to a nomination for the role at the head of the eurozone's monetary authority. Markets and eurozone governments would see a change in leadership at the bank that sets interest rates for the 20 member countries sharing the euro. Spain would gain a prominent post in European economic governance.

Reported by: Reuters. Also covered by AP, Bloomberg, The New York Times, France 24.
